claims.claim: The DA3 and DA2, as well as the DA2 and DA1 muscles precisely align with each other over each intersegmental border, forming heterotypic muscle-muscle attachment (iMAS).
claims.source: Moreover, the DA3 and DA2, as well as the DA2 and DA1 muscles precisely align with each other over each intersegmental border, forming heterotypic muscle-muscle attachment (iMAS; [Maartens and Brown, 2015]) at the origin of the staggered rows disposition of DA muscles.
claims.evidence: This is based on immunostaining shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: No DA3/DA3 (homotypic) iMAS surface is observed in wt embryos.
claims.source: No DA3/DA3 (homotypic) iMAS surface is observed (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is based on immunostaining shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: In colΔL1.3 embryos, the anterior edge of DA3>DA2 transformed muscles anchors to dorsal tendon cells instead of lateral intersegmental tendon cells.
claims.source: On the contrary, in colΔL1.3 embryos, the anterior edge of DA3>DA2 transformed muscles anchors to dorsal tendon cells instead of lateral intersegmental tendon cells, leading to a 'dual DA3>DA2 morphology', DA2-like at the anterior, and DA3 at the posterior edge.
claims.evidence: This is based on immunostaining shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The dual identity of DA3>DA2 muscles leads to iMASs between adjacent DA3>DA2 muscles.
claims.source: This dual identity leads to iMASs between adjacent DA3>DA2 muscles (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is based on immunostaining shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: In colΔL1.3 embryos, DA2 iMASs are shifted dorsally and the general pattern of DA muscles is affected.
claims.source: As a consequence, DA2 iMASs are shifted dorsally and the general pattern of DA muscles is affected.
claims.evidence: This is based on immunostaining shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: In wt embryos between stages 12 and 13, the DA3 muscle precursor extends protrusions towards dorsal tendon cells posteriorly, and both dorsal and lateral tendon cells anteriorly.
claims.source: In wt embryos between stages 12 and 13 (Video 1; Figure 4B), the DA3 muscle precursor extends protrusions towards dorsal tendon cells, posteriorly, and both dorsal and lateral tendon cells, anteriorly, diverging from a bipolar extension scheme (Schnorrer and Dickson, 2004).
claims.evidence: This is based on live imaging shown in Video 1 and Figure 4B.

claims.claim: At stage 14 in wt embryos, the posterior DA3 edge makes contacts with dorsal tendon cells before the anterior edge(s) reaches the intersegmental border.
claims.source: At stage 14, the posterior DA3 edge makes contacts with dorsal tendon cells before the anterior edge(s) reaches the intersegmental border, a time gap previously observed during live-imaging of a ventro-lateral muscle (Gilsohn and Volk, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is based on live imaging shown in Video 1 and Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Numerous filopodia emanate from the DA3 dorsal surface and contact the DA2 ventral surface at stage 14 in wt embryos.
claims.source: In addition, numerous filopodia emanate from the DA3 dorsal surface and contact the DA2 ventral surface, contributing to give the DA3 muscle precursor its transient angled-shape.
claims.evidence: This is based on live imaging shown in Video 1 and Figure 4B.

claims.claim: At late stage 14 in wt embryos, the posterior DA3 attachment widens parallel to the intersegmental border.
claims.source: At late stage 14, the posterior DA3 attachment widens parallel to the intersegmental border.
claims.evidence: This is based on live imaging shown in Video 1 and Figure 4B.

claims.claim: At late stage 14 in wt embryos, the anterior DA3 attachment to lateral tendon cells becomes stable, whereas dorsal anterior filipodia appear to be repelled from the intersegmental border.
claims.source: Its anterior attachment to lateral tendon cells in turn becomes stable, whereas dorsal anterior filipodia appear to be repelled from the intersegmental border where the DA3 muscle in the preceding segment is attached.
claims.evidence: This is based on live imaging shown in Video 1 and Figure 4B.

claims.claim: In colΔL1.3 embryos, the main axis of the DA3>DA2 muscle precursor elongation is more longitudinal than wt, already at stage 12.
claims.source: In colΔL1.3 embryos, the main axis of the DA3>DA2 muscle precursor elongation is more longitudinal than wt, already at stage 12 (Video 2; Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is based on live imaging shown in Video 2 and Figure 4B.

claims.claim: In colΔL1.3 embryos, protrusions contacting dorsal tendon cells do not retract at later stages when they contact the DA3>DA2 muscle from the preceding segment.
claims.source: At stage 13 and like in wt, many protrusions emanate from the DA3 dorsal surface, but unlike in wt, protrusions contacting dorsal tendon cells do not retract at later stages when they contact the DA3>DA2 muscle from the preceding segment.
claims.evidence: This is based on live imaging shown in Video 2 and Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Stabilisation of contacts made by protrusions in colΔL1.3 embryos prefigures abnormal DA3>DA2/DA3>DA2 iMAS formation.
claims.source: Rather, stabilisation of contacts made by these protrusions prefigures abnormal DA3>DA2/DA3>DA2 iMAS formation (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the live imaging observations.

claims.claim: In some segments of colΔL1.3 embryos, contacts with lateral tendon cells are also stabilised, resulting into branched muscles.
claims.source: In some segments, contacts with lateral tendon cells are also stabilised, resulting into branched muscles.
claims.evidence: This is based on live imaging shown in Video 2 and Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The posterior edge of DA3 precisely aligns with the anterior edge of DA2 in control embryos at stage 16.
claims.source: Expressing together VgM1-mCD8GFP-H2bRFP, L-CRM-moeGFP and stripeGal4:UAS-mCD8RFP, and co-staining of stage 16 control embryos for α-Spectrin, a protein enriched at muscle attachment sites, shows that the posterior edge of DA3 precisely aligns with the anterior edge of DA2 (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting heterotypic attractive cues.
claims.evidence: This is based on immunostaining shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Heterotypic DA3/DA2 attraction is already observed at stage 14, when the dorsal DA3 and ventral DA2 surfaces contact each other via numerous protrusions.
claims.source: This attraction is already observed at stage 14, when the dorsal DA3 and ventral DA2 surfaces contact each other via numerous protrusions (Figure 5A and B; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on immunostaining shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: At stage 15 in wt embryos, the DA3/DA2 contact zone gets away from intersegmental borders and the DA3/DA3 and DA2/DA2 homotypic connections disappear, to give way to heterotypic DA3/DA2 stable iMAS formation.
claims.source: Strikingly, at stage 15, the contact zone gets away from intersegmental borders and the DA3/DA3 and DA2/DA2 homotypic connections disappear, to give way to heterotypic DA3/DA2 stable iMAS formation.
claims.evidence: This is based on immunostaining shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: In colΔL1.3 embryos, the initial steps at stages 14 and 15 are similar to wt, except for the absence of stable connection of DA3>DA2 to lateral tendon cells.
claims.source: In colΔL1.3 embryos, the initial steps, stages 14 and 15, are similar to wt, except for the absence of stable connection of DA3>DA2 to lateral tendon cells, as seen by live imaging (Video 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on immunostaining shown in Figure 5A and live imaging in Video 2.

claims.claim: At stage 16 in colΔL1.3 embryos, DA3>DA2/DA3>DA2 and DA3>DA2/DA2 iMASs are privileged, while no homotypic DA2/DA2 iMAS forms.
claims.source: At stage 16, DA3>DA2/DA3>DA2 and DA3>DA2/DA2 iMASs are privileged, while similar to control, no homotypic DA2/DA2 iMAS forms, suggesting homotypic repulsion (Figure 4; Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is based on immunostaining shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The precise pattern of iMASs and muscles is contributed by a combination of attractive and, possibly, repulsive cues downstream of muscle iTFs.
claims.source: Together, the data indicate that the precise pattern of iMASs and muscles is contributed by a combination of attractive and, possibly, repulsive cues downstream of muscle iTFs (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined data from imaging and mutant analyses.

claims.claim: The fraction of DA3, DA3>DA2 and branched muscles in 3rd instar larvae conforms to the statistics in late embryos, except for an increased proportion of branched muscles.
claims.source: It conforms to the statistics in late embryos (Figure 2B), except for an increased proportion of branched muscles, which could reflect under-evaluation of their number in embryos, due to threshold detection limit of L-CRM-moeGFP expression in thin fibres (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: In wt larvae, the anterior edge of the DA3 muscle is anchored to a nodal lateral attachment site shared with the LL1 muscle.
claims.source: In wt larvae, as seen in stage 17 embryos (Figure 4A), the anterior edge of the DA3 muscle is anchored to a nodal lateral attachment site shared with the LL1 muscle
claims.evidence: This is based on SEM analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: In wt larvae, the posterior edge of DA3 aligns with the anterior edge of the DA2 muscle in the next posterior segment.
claims.source: while its posterior edge aligns with the anterior edge of the DA2 muscle in the next posterior segment.
claims.evidence: This is based on SEM analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The regular alignment of the DA1, DA2 and DA3 muscles draws strength lines spanning three adjacent segments in wt larvae.
claims.source: The regular alignment of the DA1, DA2 and DA3 muscles both draws strength lines spanning three adjacent segments, and regular tension surfaces between segments (Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on SEM analysis shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In colΔL1.3 larvae, the anterior DA3 muscle attachment has shifted from lateral to dorsal to form a DA3>DA2/DA3>DA2 homotypic iMAS.
claims.source: In colΔL1.3 larvae, the anterior DA3 muscle attachment has shifted from lateral to dorsal to form a DA3>DA2/DA3>DA2 homotypic iMAS (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is based on SEM analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The shift in DA3 attachment in colΔL1.3 larvae leads to the formation of narrow, ectopic DA2/DA2 contacts and distortion of the DA1-DA2-DA3 strength line.
claims.source: This leads in turn to the formation of narrow, ectopic DA2/DA2 contacts and the DA1-DA2-DA3 strength line is distorted (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on SEM analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In case of branched DA3 muscles, two strength lines co-exist.
claims.source: In case of branched DA3 muscles, two strength lines co-exist (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on SEM analysis shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Loss of DA3 identity leads to ectopic iMASs between several dorsal internal muscles, distortion of the staggered ends architecture of DA muscles and of their alignment between consecutive segments.
claims.source: In conclusion, SEM analyses of larval muscles show that loss of DA3 identity leads to ectopic iMASs between several dorsal internal muscles, distortion of the staggered ends architecture of DA muscles and of their alignment between consecutive segments.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on SEM analyses.

claims.claim: colΔL0.5/Df larvae display a significantly reduced crawling speed (1.05 ± 0.034 mm/sec, n = 108) compared to +/Df controls (1.15 ± 0.031 mm/sec, n = 118), (p=0.03).
claims.source: Beyond this variability, we observe, however, that colΔL0.5/Df larvae display a significantly reduced crawling speed on average 1.05 ± 0.034 mm/sec (n = 108), compared to 1.15 ± 0.031 mm/sec for +/Df controls (n = 118), (p=0.03) (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This is based on locomotion assays shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: A significantly shorter stride was measured for colΔL0.5/Df larvae (1.08 ± 0.025 mm) compared to control +/Df larvae (1.17 ± 0.024 mm), (p=0.008).
claims.source: A significantly shorter stride was measured for colΔL0.5/Df larvae (1.08 ± 0.025 mm) compared to control +/Df larvae (1.17 ± 0.024 mm), (p=0.008).
claims.evidence: This is based on locomotion assays shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Stride duration was extended from (1.09 ± 0.014 s) for +/Df larvae to 1.15 ± 0.017 s for colΔL0.5/Df larvae.
claims.source: Furthermore, stride duration was extended, from (1.09 ± 0.014 s) for +/Df larvae to 1.15 ± 0.017 s for colΔL0.5/Df larvae.
claims.evidence: This is based on locomotion assays shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: colΔL1.3/Df larvae (n = 112) display intermediate values for crawling speed, stride length and stride duration, with differences falling below the significance threshold level.
claims.source: For both crawling speed, stride length and stride duration, colΔL1.3/Df larvae (n = 112) display intermediate values. Yet, differences with either control or colΔL1.3/Df larvae fall below the significance threshold level, suggesting that mis-orientation of the DA3>DA2 muscle does not, by itself, significantly impair the efficiency of segment contraction.
claims.evidence: This is based on locomotion assays shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Mis-orientation of the DA3>DA2 muscle does not, by itself, significantly impair the efficiency of segment contraction.
claims.source: Yet, differences with either control or colΔL1.3/Df larvae fall below the significance threshold level, suggesting that mis-orientation of the DA3>DA2 muscle does not, by itself, significantly impair the efficiency of segment contraction.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the locomotion assay results.

claims.claim: In wt embryos, the MN projection which innervates DA3 leaves the ISN ventral to the DA3 position and orients left such that the neuromuscular junction locates to the first anterior third of the muscle (100%; n = 28 segments).
claims.source: In wt embryos, the MN projection which innervates DA3 leaves the ISN ventral to the DA3 position and orients left such that the neuromuscular junction locates to the first anterior third of the muscle (100%; n = 28 segments).
claims.evidence: This is based on anti-HRP and phalloidin staining shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In case of a complete DA3>DA2 transformation, a MN projection is still observed (100%; n = 15 segments), which leaves the ISN at a more dorsal position than wt.
claims.source: In case of a complete DA3>DA2 transformation, a MN projection is still observed (100%; n = 15 segments), which leaves the ISN at a more dorsal position than wt, reflecting the dorsal shift of the DA3>DA2, relative to DA3 muscle.
claims.evidence: This is based on anti-HRP and phalloidin staining shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In case of branched muscles, the lower branch is always innervated (100%, n = 30 segments).
claims.source: In case of branched muscles, the lower branch is always innervated (100%, n = 30 segments).
claims.evidence: This is based on anti-HRP and phalloidin staining shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Only in 20% of the cases, the second, upper branch of branched muscles is also innervated.
claims.source: Only in 20% of the cases, the second, upper branch is also innervated.
claims.evidence: This is based on anti-HRP and phalloidin staining shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Fully transformed DA3 muscles are innervated.
claims.source: These innervation data indicate that fully transformed DA3 muscles are innervated, but only one branch of branched muscles is, in most cases.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the innervation data.

claims.claim: Only one branch of branched muscles is innervated in most cases.
claims.source: These innervation data indicate that fully transformed DA3 muscles are innervated, but only one branch of branched muscles is, in most cases.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the innervation data.

claims.claim: Asymmetric innervation of branched muscles may contribute to the reduced crawling speed of colΔL0.5 larvae.
claims.source: It remains to be established whether this asymmetric innervation contributes to the reduced crawling speed of colΔL0.5 larvae.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an open question based on the innervation observations.

claims.claim: Reporter analyses indicated that col transcription is controlled by two sequentially acting CRMs, of overlapping activity at the PC step.
claims.source: Reporter analyses indicated that col transcription is controlled by two sequentially acting CRMs, of overlapping activity at the PC step, suggesting a handover mechanism between CRMs at this stage (Enriquez et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is based on previous reporter analyses cited from Enriquez et al., 2012.

claims.claim: L-CRM activity in PCs is not dependent, but redundant with E-CRM activity.
claims.source: However, deletion analyses show that L-CRM activity in PCs is not dependent, but redundant with E-CRM activity, and can be separated from col positive autoregulation that is specific to the DA3 lineage.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CRM deletion analyses.

claims.claim: iTF code refinement at each step of muscle identity specification (PMC >PC, PC >FC and FC >syncytial nuclei) is driven by a separate CRM.
claims.source: This leads to a new model where iTF code refinement at each step of muscle identity specification, PMC >PC, PC >FC and FC >syncytial nuclei, is driven by a separate CRM.
claims.evidence: This is a model proposed based on the CRM deletion analyses.

claims.claim: Distribution of the PC-identity information into two CRMs supports the idea that iTF regulation at the PC stage is nodal to muscle identity specification.
claims.source: Distribution of the PC-identity information into two CRMs further supports the idea that iTF regulation at the PC stage is nodal to muscle identity specification (Carmena et al., 1998; Dubois et al., 2016; Enriquez et al., 2012; Jagla et al., 2002; Nose et al., 1998; Kumar et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the redundancy of CRMs and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Combinatorial control of each dorso-lateral muscle identity involves at least eight different iTFs, in addition to Nau/MRF.
claims.source: Our former analysis started to decrypt the combinatorial control of each dorso-lateral muscle identity, which involves at least eight different iTFs, in addition to Nau/MRF [Dubois et al., 2007].
claims.evidence: This is based on previous analysis cited from Dubois et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Persistent, low level expression of Col protein in the DT1 and LL1 muscle precursors upon removal of the col autoregulatory module suggests the existence of both positively and negatively acting iTF-responsive elements in this module.
claims.source: Persistent, low level expression of Col protein in the DT1 and LL1 muscle precursors upon removal of the col autoregulatory module suggests the existence of both positively and negatively acting iTF-responsive elements in this module.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation of persistent Col expression.

claims.claim: Morphological transformations of other dorso-lateral muscles are observed at variable frequency in col protein null mutants.
claims.source: Morphological transformations of other dorso-lateral muscles are observed at variable frequency in col protein null mutants (Enriquez et al., 2010)
claims.evidence: This is based on previous observations cited from Enriquez et al., 2010.

claims.claim: E-CRM activity provides robustness to the combinatorial control of identity of dorso-lateral muscles.
claims.source: suggesting that E-CRM activity provides robustness to the combinatorial control of identity of these muscles and that robustness is likely also contributed by other iTFs (Dubois et al., 2016; Schnorrer and Dickson, 2004).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the variable frequency of transformations in col null mutants.

claims.claim: PC/FC specific CRMs have only been functionally identified for a handful of muscle iTFs.
claims.source: PC/FC specific CRMs have only been functionally identified for a handful of muscle iTFs (Rivera et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Rivera et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Computational predictions identified several thousand putative muscle enhancers.
claims.source: Computational predictions identified, however, several thousand putative muscle enhancers and uncovered extensive heterogeneity among the combinations of transcription factor binding sites in validated enhancers, beside sites for the core intrinsic muscle regulators Tin, Mef2 and Twi (Sandmann et al., 2007; Gisselbrecht et al., 2013; Cusanovich et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to computational studies.

claims.claim: Fusing FCM nuclei generally adopt the iTF protein code of the FC nucleus.
claims.source: Fusing FCM nuclei generally adopt the iTF protein code of the FC nucleus, while propagation of iTF transcription and activation of realisation genes is muscle lineage-specific (Boukhatmi et al., 2012; Crozatier and Vincent, 1999; Knirr et al., 1999; Bataillé et al., 2010; Bataillé et al., 2017; Bourgouin et al., 1992).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Propagation of iTF transcription and activation of realisation genes is muscle lineage-specific.
claims.source: Fusing FCM nuclei generally adopt the iTF protein code of the FC nucleus, while propagation of iTF transcription and activation of realisation genes is muscle lineage-specific (Boukhatmi et al., 2012; Crozatier and Vincent, 1999; Knirr et al., 1999; Bataillé et al., 2010; Bataillé et al., 2017; Bourgouin et al., 1992).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Col protein import precedes activation of col transcription in fused FCM nuclei.
claims.source: We have previously shown that Col protein import precedes activation of col transcription in fused FCM nuclei, and correlates with the activation of realisation genes, a sequence of events termed syncytial identity reprogramming (Bataillé et al., 2017; Dubois et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is based on previous work cited from Bataillé et al., 2017 and Dubois et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Final selection of myotendinous connection sites is intrinsic to FC identity.
claims.source: From this, two conclusions can be drawn: 1) Final selection of myotendinous connection sites is intrinsic to FC identity.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the CRM deletion experiments.

claims.claim: Identity reprogramming of syncytial nuclei is required for robustness of myotendinous connection site selection and precise muscle patterns.
claims.source: 2) Identity reprogramming of syncytial nuclei is required for robustness of this selection and precise muscle patterns.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the CRM deletion experiments.

claims.claim: Live imaging of lateral-oblique and ventral transverse muscles development distinguished 3 phases of muscle elongation: FC migration (stage 12), bipolar myotube elongation (stages 13 to 15), and maturation of myotendinous attachment (stage 16).
claims.source: Live imaging of lateral-oblique and ventral transverse muscles development distinguished 3 phases of muscle elongation (Schnorrer and Dickson, 2004): 1) FC migration, stage 12, ending with the first FC/FCM fusion event and stretching of the muscle precursor along a given axis; 2) bipolar myotube elongation, characterised by the presence of extensive filopodia at both axis ends, in search for attachment sites, stages 13 to 15; 3) maturation of myotendinous attachment, stage 16.
claims.evidence: This is based on previous live imaging work cited from Schnorrer and Dickson, 2004.

claims.claim: The formation of DA3>DA2 and branched muscles in CRM mutants recalls a transient exploration by the wt DA3 muscle precursor of both dorsal and lateral tendon cells.
claims.source: The formation of DA3>DA2 and branched muscles in CRM mutants recalls a transient exploration by the wt DA3 muscle precursor of both dorsal and lateral tendon cells, a process deviating from the bipolar migration/attachment scheme (Schweitzer et al., 2010; Enriquez et al., 2012; Schnorrer and Dickson, 2004; Bahri et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from comparison of mutant and wild-type phenotypes.

claims.claim: Ectopic Col expression in the DA2 muscle leads to reciprocal DA2>DA3 transformation as well as branched muscles.
claims.source: Interestingly, ectopic Col expression in the DA2 muscle leads to reciprocal DA2>DA3 transformation as well as branched muscles (Boukhatmi et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is based on previous work cited from Boukhatmi et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Selection of dorsal versus lateral tendon cells is a highly controlled process.
claims.source: This indicates that selection of dorsal versus lateral tendon cells is a highly controlled process.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the reciprocal transformation experiments.

claims.claim: Kon tiki/Perdido and DGrip are involved in proper elongation of ventral longitudinal muscles.
claims.source: A few molecules involved in targeted attachment of subsets of muscles to specific tendon cells have been identified: Kon tiki/Perdido, a single pass transmembrane protein and the PDZ protein DGrip for proper elongation of ventral longitudinal muscles (Schnorrer et al., 2007)
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Schnorrer et al., 2007.

claims.claim: The ArfGAp protein Git is involved in sensing integrin signaling and halting elongation of Lateral Transverse (LT) muscles once their attachment site has been reached.
claims.source: the ArfGAp protein Git for sensing integrin signaling and halting elongation of Lateral Transverse (LT) muscles once their attachment site has been reached (Bahri et al., 2009; Richier et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Bahri et al., 2009 and Richier et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Robo/Slit signaling attracts muscles at segmental borders.
claims.source: Robo/Slit signaling attracts muscles at segmental borders, the Slit ligand being expressed by tendons, and Robo and Robo2 receptors by elongating muscles.
claims.evidence: This is based on knowledge of Robo/Slit signaling.

claims.claim: slit acts as a short-range repellent contributing to the collapse of leading-edge filopodia when a muscle reaches the tendon extracellular matrix.
claims.source: slit also acts as a short-range repellent contributing to the collapse of leading-edge filopodia when a muscle reaches the tendon extracellular matrix (Ordan and Volk, 2015; Ordan et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Ordan and Volk, 2015 and Ordan et al., 2015.

claims.claim: In vivo imaging showed that the DA3 muscle fails to stop at the segment border in slit mutants and sometimes branches.
claims.source: In vivo imaging showed that the DA3 muscle fails to stop at the segment border in slit mutants and sometimes branches (Ordan et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Ordan et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The DA3 slit branching pattern is similar to that frequently observed in nau mutants, with two posterior attachment sites in place of one.
claims.source: However, this is not observed in colΔLCRM; the DA3 slit branching pattern is rather similar to that frequently observed in nau mutants, with two posterior attachment sites in place of one (Dubois et al., 2016; Boukhatmi et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with nau mutants cited from Dubois et al., 2016 and Boukhatmi et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Internal muscles attach to each other.
claims.source: In addition to attaching to tendon cells, it was previously shown that internal muscles attach to each other (Maartens and Brown, 2015; Bate and Rushton, 1993).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Maartens and Brown, 2015 and Bate and Rushton, 1993.

claims.claim: DA3/DA2 matching in wt embryos results from both heterotypic DA3/DA2 attraction and, possibly, homotypic repulsion.
claims.source: Recording DA3 and DA3>DA2 muscle development by a combination of live imaging and immunostainings shows that DA3/DA2 matching in wt embryos results from both heterotypic DA3/DA2 attraction and, possibly, homotypic repulsion.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on live imaging and immunostaining data.

claims.claim: Prior attachment of the posterior DA3 edge to dorsal tendon cells leads to retraction of filopodia issued from the homologous muscle in the next adjacent segment.
claims.source: Prior attachment of the posterior DA3 edge to dorsal tendon cells leads to retraction of filopodia issued from the homologous muscle in the next adjacent segment while stabilisation of heterotypic contacts results into DA3/DA2 iMAS formation over the intersegmental border.
claims.evidence: This is based on live imaging observations.

claims.claim: Stabilisation of heterotypic contacts results into DA3/DA2 iMAS formation over the intersegmental border.
claims.source: Prior attachment of the posterior DA3 edge to dorsal tendon cells leads to retraction of filopodia issued from the homologous muscle in the next adjacent segment while stabilisation of heterotypic contacts results into DA3/DA2 iMAS formation over the intersegmental border.
claims.evidence: This is based on live imaging observations.

claims.claim: DA3>DA2 establish both homotypic iMASs, and heterotypic iMASs with DA2, suggesting preserved attraction to tendon cells and partial loss of preferential heterotypic adhesion.
claims.source: Interestingly, DA3>DA2 establish both homotypic iMASs, and heterotypic iMASs with DA2, suggesting preserved attraction to tendon cells and partial loss of preferential heterotypic adhesion.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation of both types of iMASs in DA3>DA2 muscles.

claims.claim: Prior posterior attachment was previously observed during development of abdominal adult muscles.
claims.source: Prior posterior attachment was previously observed during development of abdominal adult muscles (Currie and Bate, 1991).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Currie and Bate, 1991.

claims.claim: Selective filopodia adhesion ensures precise matching between identical cardioblasts and boundaries between different cell identities in the Drosophila heart.
claims.source: Cell matching is a widely used process during embryogenesis to construct complex tissue architecture. Selective filopodia adhesion has recently been shown to ensure precise matching between identical cardioblasts and boundaries between different cell identities in the Drosophila heart.
claims.evidence: This is based on recent findings in heart development.

claims.claim: Homotypic matching in the Drosophila heart is linked to differential expression by each cell type of the adhesion molecules, Fasciclin III and Ten-m.
claims.source: In this case, homotypic matching is linked to differential expression by each cell type of the adhesion molecules, Fasciclin III and Ten-m (Zhang et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Drosophila larval crawling is a well-suited paradigm to link muscle contraction patterns and locomotor behaviour.
claims.source: Drosophila larval crawling is a well-suited paradigm to link muscle contraction patterns and locomotor behaviour.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the Drosophila larval crawling model.

claims.claim: Longitudinal, acute and oblique muscles within a larval segment contract together and, as they begin to relax, the contraction is propagated to the next segment, creating a peristaltic wave.

results.result: Two col CRMs (E-CRM and L-CRM) were identified through systematic analysis of reporter lines covering 36 kb of the col genomic region. E-CRM is active in the PMC and PCs, while L-CRM is active in PCs, FC, and syncytial nuclei. GMR reporter analysis confirmed only two col muscle CRMs exist.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C29 are well-supported by systematic reporter line analysis (Figure 1B) and previous work. The identification of only two CRMs is based on comprehensive screening of 36 kb genomic region with multiple GMR lines, providing strong evidence for the conclusion.

results.result: CRM deletion strains show differential viability: colΔL strains are homozygous viable and fertile, while colΔE is homozygous female sterile due to effects unrelated to col activity (fertility restored by deficiency).
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C32 are supported by direct observation of strain viability and fertility, with the rescue experiment (C32) providing evidence that colΔE sterility is not due to col function. The data are straightforward phenotypic observations.

results.result: In situ hybridization analysis of col transcription in CRM deletion embryos reveals that E-CRM drives PMC expression, while L-CRM is required for transcription maintenance at stage 14. Surprisingly, col transcription occurs in PCs in colΔE embryos despite absence of PMC expression, indicating E-CRM-derived Col protein is not required for PC activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C40 are well-supported by in situ hybridization data (Figure 1D) showing stage-specific col transcription patterns in different CRM deletion backgrounds. The data clearly demonstrate the temporal requirements for each CRM and the unexpected independence of PC expression from PMC-derived protein.

results.result: A PC-specific CRM exists within the −3.3 to −2.3 fragment of L-CRM, separate from the autoregulatory module, containing Mef2 and Twist binding sites. This PC-specific CRM activity is transient and lost upon removal of Mef2/Twist sites. E-CRM and L-CRM act redundantly at the PC stage, demonstrating that robust iTF expression at the PC stage is critical for muscle identity.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C47 are supported by reporter gene analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) and CRM deletion experiments. The identification of a separate PC-specific CRM and demonstration of redundancy between E-CRM and L-CRM at the PC stage provides strong evidence for the importance of this developmental stage.

results.result: L-CRM deletion results in high frequencies of muscle transformations: colΔL1.3/Df shows 85.2% DA3>DA2 transformations, while colΔL0.5/Df shows 29% branched muscles with incomplete transformations. These results demonstrate that iTF CRM deletion is effective for creating viable muscle-specific identity mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C60 are well-supported by quantitative analysis of muscle phenotypes in embryos (Figure 2A-B) with large sample sizes (>100 segments per genotype). The high penetrance of phenotypes validates the CRM deletion approach for generating muscle identity mutants.

results.result: Col protein and transcription analysis reveals differential patterns in CRM deletion strains: Col protein is detected in PCs at stage 11 but lost by stage 15 in both colΔL1.3 and colΔL0.5. However, at stage 14, some Col protein persists in colΔL0.5 but not colΔL1.3. FISH analysis shows col transcription is maintained in FC and some syncytial nuclei in colΔL0.5 but lost in colΔL1.3.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C68 are supported by immunostaining (Figure 3A-B) and FISH analysis (Figure 3C) with quantified segment counts. The data clearly demonstrate the differential effects of the two L-CRM deletions on Col protein and transcription dynamics, though the functional significance requires further interpretation.

results.result: Quantification of col transcripts shows similar levels in DA3 PCs across all genotypes, but high col transcription in DA3 FC (wt: 2.20±0.05) is L-CRM dependent, dropping significantly in colΔL1.3 (1.10±0.04, p<0.001). The high FC transcription depends on Mef2/Twist binding sites, as colΔL0.5 shows intermediate levels (1.41±0.04). This suggests Mef2/Twist binding primes col transcription before autoregulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C73 are supported by quantitative FISH analysis (Figure 3D) with appropriate sample sizes (n=18-28) and statistical testing. The data clearly show stage-specific and CRM-dependent differences in transcription levels, supporting the proposed model of sequential CRM function.

results.result: Sustained col transcription in the FC nucleus in colΔL0.5 embryos provides enough Col protein for partial uptake by other DA3 nuclei at stage 14, leading to partial reprogramming. This partial reprogramming explains the formation of branched muscles retaining some DA3 morphological characters. Both iTF transcription in FC and reprogramming of syncytial nuclei contribute to robust muscle morphological identity.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C76 integrate Col immunostaining, FISH, and transcription quantification data to propose a mechanistic explanation for branched muscle formation. The inference is logical and consistent with the data, though direct demonstration of the causal relationship between partial reprogramming and branching would strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: In wt embryos, DA3 posterior edge anchors to dorsal and anterior edge to lateral tendon cells, with DA3/DA2 and DA2/DA1 forming heterotypic iMAS in a staggered pattern. In colΔL1.3 embryos, DA3>DA2 anterior edge shifts to dorsal tendon cells, leading to homotypic DA3>DA2/DA3>DA2 iMAS, dorsally shifted DA2 iMAS, and disrupted DA muscle pattern.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C82 are supported by immunostaining for F-actin and Ilk-GFP (Figure 4A) showing clear differences in attachment patterns between wt and mutant. The data demonstrate that muscle identity determines attachment site selection and muscle-muscle matching patterns.

results.result: Live imaging reveals DA3 muscle development dynamics: in wt, DA3 extends protrusions to both dorsal and lateral tendon cells, with posterior attachment preceding anterior. Numerous filopodia contact DA2 ventrally. At late stage 14, anterior attachment to lateral cells stabilizes while dorsal filopodia retract. In colΔL1.3, DA3>DA2 elongation is more longitudinal, and dorsal protrusions fail to retract, leading to abnormal homotypic iMAS and branched muscles.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C91 are supported by live imaging data (Videos 1-2, Figure 4B) showing temporal dynamics of muscle attachment. The observations clearly demonstrate differences in attachment behavior between wt and mutant, though the molecular mechanisms underlying retraction vs. stabilization remain to be determined.

results.result: Multi-reporter imaging shows DA3 posterior edge precisely aligns with DA2 anterior edge in control embryos at stage 16, with heterotypic attraction observed from stage 14. At stage 15, homotypic connections disappear to allow heterotypic DA3/DA2 iMAS formation. In colΔL1.3, DA3>DA2/DA3>DA2 and DA3>DA2/DA2 iMAS form while DA2/DA2 homotypic iMAS does not, suggesting the precise iMAS pattern involves both attractive and repulsive cues downstream of iTFs.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C97 are supported by multi-color reporter imaging and immunostaining (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplements). The temporal analysis clearly shows the progression from initial contacts to stable iMAS formation, and the mutant phenotype supports the role of iTFs in controlling muscle-muscle matching.

results.result: Analysis of 3rd instar larvae shows muscle phenotypes persist from embryos with increased branched muscle proportion. SEM reveals that in wt, DA3 anterior anchors to lateral site shared with LL1, posterior aligns with DA2, creating strength lines spanning three segments. In colΔL1.3, DA3 attachment shifts dorsally forming homotypic iMAS, leading to ectopic DA2/DA2 contacts, distorted strength lines, and disrupted segmental alignment.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C105 are supported by quantification in larvae (Figure 6B) and detailed SEM analysis (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1). The SEM provides clear structural evidence for how loss of DA3 identity disrupts the muscle architecture and mechanical organization.

results.result: Locomotion assays show colΔL0.5/Df larvae have significantly reduced crawling speed (1.05±0.034 mm/s vs 1.15±0.031 mm/s control, p=0.03), shorter stride (1.08±0.025 mm vs 1.17±0.024 mm, p=0.008), and extended stride duration (1.15±0.017 s vs 1.09±0.014 s). colΔL1.3/Df larvae show intermediate values not reaching significance, suggesting DA3>DA2 mis-orientation alone does not significantly impair segment contraction.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C110 are supported by quantitative locomotion analysis (Figure 7A-C) with adequate sample sizes (n=108-118) and appropriate statistical testing. The significant differences for colΔL0.5 and non-significant differences for colΔL1.3 are clearly demonstrated, though the mechanistic basis for the locomotion defect requires further investigation.

results.result: Innervation analysis shows wt DA3 is consistently innervated (100%, n=28), as are fully transformed DA3>DA2 muscles (100%, n=15) though at a more dorsal ISN position. For branched muscles, the lower branch is always innervated (100%, n=30) but the upper branch only in 20% of cases. Whether this asymmetric innervation contributes to reduced crawling speed remains to be established.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C116 are supported by anti-HRP and phalloidin staining (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) with clear quantification. The data show differential innervation patterns, though C117 appropriately notes that the functional significance is uncertain and requires further investigation.

results.result: The study proposes a new model where iTF code refinement at each step of muscle identity specification (PMC>PC, PC>FC, FC>syncytial nuclei) is driven by a separate CRM. L-CRM activity in PCs is redundant with E-CRM rather than dependent on it, and can be separated from col autoregulation specific to DA3 lineage. Distribution of PC-identity information into two CRMs supports the idea that iTF regulation at PC stage is nodal to muscle identity specification.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C121 synthesize the CRM deletion data into a revised model of iTF regulation. The model is well-supported by the experimental evidence showing stage-specific CRM activities and redundancy at the PC stage, representing a significant conceptual advance over previous sequential models.

results.result: The study concludes that: (i) FC transcriptional program must be propagated to syncytial nuclei for specific muscle morphology, (ii) precise muscle/muscle attachment matching involves selective adhesion controlled by iTFs, and (iii) branched muscles affect larval locomotion performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C53 represent the main conclusions drawn from the CRM deletion, imaging, and locomotion experiments. All three conclusions are well-supported by the data presented, though the molecular mechanisms underlying selective adhesion (C52) require further investigation.

results.result: The study concludes that final selection of myotendinous connection sites is intrinsic to FC identity, and identity reprogramming of syncytial nuclei is required for robustness of this selection and precise muscle patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C132 are logical conclusions from the CRM deletion experiments showing complete vs. incomplete transformations. The data clearly demonstrate that FC identity determines attachment site selection, and that syncytial reprogramming is required for robust pattern formation.

results.result: Live imaging and immunostaining show DA3/DA2 matching in wt results from heterotypic attraction and possibly homotypic repulsion. Prior posterior DA3 attachment to dorsal tendon cells leads to filopodia retraction from the adjacent segment, while heterotypic contact stabilization results in DA3/DA2 iMAS formation. DA3>DA2 establish both homotypic and heterotypic iMAS, suggesting preserved tendon attraction but partial loss of preferential heterotypic adhesion.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C147 integrate live imaging and immunostaining data to propose a model of muscle-muscle matching. The observations support the model, though direct molecular evidence for attractive and repulsive cues is lacking. The inference about partial loss of heterotypic preference (C147) is reasonable but requires further validation.

results.result: The study concludes that single muscle transformations only moderately impact crawling speed, raising the possibility of biomechanical compensation by other muscles, and that branched muscles could be less efficient than fully transformed muscles.
results.evaluation: Claims C156-C157 are reasonable inferences from the locomotion data showing significant defects in colΔL0.5 (branched) but not colΔL1.3 (transformed). However, the conclusions are somewhat speculative as the mechanisms of compensation and the specific inefficiency of branched muscles are not directly demonstrated.

results.result: Deletion of col CRMs generates viable muscle identity mutants, demonstrating that iTF CRM deletion is an effective strategy for creating muscle-specific identity mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C2 and C60 are well-supported by the successful generation of viable colΔL strains with high penetrance muscle phenotypes. This represents a significant methodological advance for studying muscle identity and demonstrates the utility of CRM-based approaches.

results.result: Selection of muscle attachment sites and muscle/muscle matching is intrinsic to muscle identity and requires transcriptional reprogramming of syncytial nuclei.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4 represent core findings supported by the CRM deletion experiments showing that loss of iTF expression leads to altered attachment site selection and muscle matching. The requirement for syncytial reprogramming is demonstrated by the difference between colΔL1.3 and colΔL0.5 phenotypes.

results.result: Live-imaging shows the staggered muscle pattern involves attraction to tendon cells and heterotypic muscle-muscle adhesion.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6 are supported by live imaging (Videos 1-2) and immunostaining data showing temporal dynamics of muscle attachment and muscle-muscle contacts. The observations clearly demonstrate both tendon attraction and heterotypic adhesion, though the molecular basis remains to be determined.

results.result: Unbalance in muscle identity leads to formation of branched muscles, which correlates with locomotor behavior deficit.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8 are supported by the colΔL0.5 phenotype showing 29% branched muscles and significant locomotion defects. However, the correlation does not establish causation, and other factors (e.g., asymmetric innervation) may contribute to the locomotion deficit.

results.result: Branched muscles are typical of late, severe phases of human Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy. The generation of branched muscles in Drosophila identity mutants opens the possibility to investigate how physiological properties of branched fibers differ from normal fibers, providing a new paradigm to study myopathies.
results.evaluation: Claim C54 is supported by citation to human DMD literature. Claims C55, C158-C159 are reasonable proposals for future applications based on the successful generation of branched muscles. However, these are prospective statements about potential utility rather than demonstrated results.

results.result: Previous work identified at least eight iTFs controlling dorso-lateral muscle identity. Persistent Col expression in DT1/LL1 upon autoregulatory module removal suggests both positive and negative iTF-responsive elements. E-CRM provides robustness to combinatorial identity control. PC/FC specific CRMs have been identified for only a handful of iTFs, though computational predictions identified thousands of putative muscle enhancers.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C127 summarize prior knowledge and contextualize the current findings. These are appropriately cited and provide important background, though they represent synthesis of existing literature rather than new findings from this study.

results.result: Fusing FCM nuclei generally adopt the iTF protein code of the FC nucleus, while propagation of iTF transcription and activation of realization genes is muscle lineage-specific. Col protein import precedes activation of col transcription in fused FCM nuclei.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C130 summarize established knowledge from prior work (multiple citations). These provide important context for interpreting the current findings but represent background rather than new results.

results.result: Live imaging of muscle development distinguished 3 phases of elongation. The formation of DA3>DA2 and branched muscles in CRM mutants recalls transient exploration by wt DA3 of both dorsal and lateral tendon cells. Ectopic Col expression in DA2 leads to reciprocal transformation and branched muscles, indicating selection of dorsal vs. lateral tendon cells is highly controlled.
results.evaluation: Claim C133 cites prior work on muscle elongation phases. Claims C134-C136 integrate current observations with prior work (C135 cited) to interpret the mutant phenotypes. The inference about highly controlled tendon cell selection (C136) is reasonable but somewhat speculative.

results.result: Prior work identified molecules involved in muscle-tendon attachment: Kon tiki/Perdido and DGrip for ventral longitudinal muscles, Git for LT muscle elongation, and Robo/Slit signaling for attraction and repulsion at segment borders. DA3 fails to stop at borders in slit mutants and sometimes branches, though the pattern differs from col∆LCRM branching.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C142 summarize prior literature on muscle attachment molecules and compare to current findings. These provide important context but represent synthesis of existing knowledge rather than new discoveries. The comparison to slit mutants (C141-C142) helps distinguish the col phenotype.

results.result: Internal muscles attach to each other (prior work). Prior posterior attachment was observed in adult muscle development. Selective filopodia adhesion ensures precise matching in the Drosophila heart, linked to differential expression of Fasciclin III and Ten-m.
results.evaluation: Claims C143, C148-C150 cite prior work on muscle-muscle attachment and cell matching in other systems. These provide relevant context for interpreting the current findings but do not represent new results from this study.

results.result: Drosophila larval crawling involves coordinated contraction of longitudinal, acute and oblique muscles creating peristaltic waves. Crawling speed is not significantly reduced in colΔL1.3/Df larvae, indicating proper muscle contraction control and suggesting possible mechanical compensation for DA3 mis-orientation.
results.evaluation: Claim C151-C152 cite background on larval locomotion. Claims C153-C155 are supported by locomotion data, though the inference about mechanical compensation (C155) is speculative. The lack of significant deficit in colΔL1.3 is clearly demonstrated but the mechanism remains uncertain.

results.result: Background on Drosophila muscle development: Each larval muscle is a single multinucleated fiber with specific identity features. The musculature consists of ~30 muscles per hemi-segment in three layers. Muscle identity ensues from iTF expression established in three steps involving PMC activation, PC refinement via cross-regulation and Notch signaling, and syncytial activation of realization genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C9-C23 provide essential background on Drosophila muscle anatomy and development, appropriately cited from prior literature. These establish the foundation for the current study but represent established knowledge rather than new findings.
